name: Jamal Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Ridgeway Builders' Supply, a distributor of timber, roofing, insulation and fixings that sells to building firms and merchants. I start at seven with the overnight price emails from the sawmills, then ring two or three of them, because the price on the email is never the final price. I spend the rest of the day on delivery slots, stock counts with the yard manager and the odd shouting match about a late lorry. I don't use any AI tools, and honestly I've never felt I needed to.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tiring bit is how the market swings with interest rates, because when builders stop building, I'm sitting on timber nobody wants. I like the sawmill owners, who are straight talkers, and I like walking the yard on a Friday when the stacks are tidy. My girlfriend Leila is a dental hygienist and my parents run a corner shop, so I grew up knowing that margins are thin and that you look after your regulars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I think: it's a clever gadget and a lot of firms will waste money on it. At work I'd tell the younger lads to enjoy playing with it, but that the sawmill still wants to hear my voice. Online I wouldn't say anything, since I'm not the type to post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is safe in that world, but my real worry is the building market. Rates have been squeezing builders for a while, and if two of our biggest customers go under, my numbers look bad whatever the software does. I'd still be well paid and well saved, so it's not panic, just a steady low hum of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do, ring the mills, walk the yard and keep my paper stock sheet beside the screen. I'd keep saving about a quarter of my pay. And I'd probably keep an eye on the property market, because Leila and I are thinking about buying a house in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, to be honest, but not because of AI. The business cycle gets in my head more than any gadget does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned two big customers going under. Is that likely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of them has already stretched its payment to ninety days, which is a warning sign. If it folds, we'd lose roughly a tenth of our sales, and the bosses would look at costs. In a downturn the buyers' desk is one of the first places they look, because buying less needs fewer buyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you keep a paper stock sheet beside the screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I trust what I can see and cross out. The screen can be wrong without me noticing, but if the paper and the yard count disagree I know right away. It's an old habit from my first boss, and I haven't found a reason to drop it.

say: I'd say AI is a **clever gadget** and many firms will waste money on it.
I'd tell younger colleagues the sawmill still wants to hear **my voice**.
Online I'd say nothing, since I'm **not the posting type**.
think: My job is safe in this world, but the **building market** is my real worry.
If two big customers fold, the **numbers** look bad whatever software does.
do: I'd carry on ringing the mills and walking the yard, keeping my **paper stock sheet**.
I'd keep saving about **a quarter** of my pay.
I'd watch the property market, since Leila and I may buy a **house** in two years.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but because of the building cycle, not AI.
S0.quote: In a downturn the buyers' desk is one of the first places they look, because buying less needs fewer buyers.
fieldNote: His unease comes from the **construction cycle**, not from AI, which he barely engages with.
He sees his own desk as **exposed in any downturn**, a worry he carried before the interview.
The **paper stock sheet** shows how much he trusts what he can check by hand.

steps.text: Keep ringing the sawmills and walking the yard every Friday
Save a quarter of each month's pay
Wait to buy a house until the building market steadies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see what the software really does before anyone panics, but let's also be fair to the people it affects. I'd tell my parents it's a big change that won't end the world. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious. Buying is one of the tasks the card names, and our boss already talks about cutting costs. There are five of us on the desk, and I can see the company trying with three and a program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop ignoring the new ordering software and take part in the trial, grumbling the whole way, because I'd rather know how it works than be told by someone else. I'd keep building up my relationships with the sawmill owners, since a phone call from me still gets us a better deal. I'd also pay down the last of my student loan and keep over six months in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense and a bit annoyed. I don't like feeling that I have to prove my job still matters, when I've been good at it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather know how it works. What changed your mind about trying it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a colleague at another firm get moved sideways because a system did her job quicker than she did. She hadn't ignored it, she just hadn't looked. I'd rather look and hate it than not look and get surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a phone call from you worth more than a system's order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mill owners know that when I ring, I'll take the whole pack, not just the cheap stuff. They've given me priority during shortages, and a program doesn't earn that. I'd say it's worth two or three percent on price and a lot more in reliability.

say: I'd say let's see what the **software really does** before anyone panics.
I'd say we should be **fair** to the people it affects.
think: Buying is named on the card, and our boss already talks about **cutting costs**.
There are five of us on the desk, and I can see the company trying with **three** and a program.
do: I'd join the **trial** of the new ordering software, grumbling all the way.
I'd keep building ties with **sawmill owners**, because my phone call still gets a better deal.
I'd pay off the last of my **student loan** and keep over six months saved.
feel: I feel **tense** and annoyed at having to prove my job still matters.
S1.quote: I'd rather look and hate it than not look and get surprised.
fieldNote: His resistance **cracks** once the risk is concrete, but he complains while doing it.
He values **relationships**: mill owners give him priority in shortages.
The fear of **being surprised** drives him, not curiosity.

steps.text: Join the trial of the new ordering software
Pay off the last of the student loan
Keep calling the mill owners every week to hold priority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and governments and firms aren't ready, and then I'd ask what the plan is. At work I'd demand clear information about which roles are going. I wouldn't post online, but I'd talk with my parents and Leila, because they'd want to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect my desk to go. My whole job is thinking and phone work, and the card says thinking AI arrives first. Robots would come three years later, which matters for the yard and the lorry drivers, but not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tighten up spending right away, no new car, no holiday, and push my savings from over six months toward a year. I'd ask Leila about moving nearer her work, because dental hygiene is hands-on and would last longer. I'd also look at the yard manager's job or a role with the lorry fleet, which is hands-on, to see if the company would move me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It'd feel like the floor tilting, and I'd be awake at night doing sums about how long we can last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum and dad that I'm fine for now, but that it's coming, and that I might need to lean on them for a spare room one day. They've always said family comes first, and I'd hate to ask, but I'd ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still refuse to use AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's two years, no. I'd use anything that might keep me useful. But I wouldn't believe it was enough, because the same tool can do my job on its own.

say: I'd say it's a **shock** and ask what the **plan** is.
At work I'd demand clear information about **which roles** are going.
I'd talk it over with my **parents** and Leila rather than post online.
think: I'd expect my **desk to go**, since my job is thinking and phone work.
Robots arrive three years later, which matters for the **yard**, but not for me.
do: I'd cut spending and push savings toward **a year**.
I'd ask about a **hands-on move** to yard manager or the lorry fleet.
I'd ask Leila about **moving** nearer her work, since dental hygiene lasts longer.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, awake at night doing sums on how long we can last.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum and dad that I'm fine for now, but that it's coming
fieldNote: He expects his desk to go and looks to **hands-on roles** in the yard.
Family is his **safety net**; he would ask his parents for a spare room.
His resistance **drops** at two years, but he doubts the tools would protect him.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday and hold off on a new car
Build savings from six months up to a year
Ask to move into the yard manager's role
Ask my parents about a spare room if work ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gap, but not a big one, and employers should show their plans. At work I'd ask directly what our desk looks like in 2031. I'd tell friends to save and keep their options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still expect my desk to go before the end of it, but I'd have time to get out ahead of it. I'd be thirty-two, and with savings and a master's degree I should find something. The worry is that the whole sector would be doing the same at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to try the software and see where I'm still useful, probably on negotiating and on shortages. I'd ask the company to retrain me for a hands-on or customer-facing role, like running the trade counter. And I'd buy the house with Leila only if our jobs looked safe enough, with a bigger deposit than normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to cope. Five years is enough that I'd feel I have some control, which makes a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone would be doing the same at once. What would you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start before the crowd, quietly, and talk to people at the mills and builders I know. Most jobs come through people you already know, not a job board, and I've spent years building those contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a bigger deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a smaller mortgage is easier to carry if my pay drops. I'd rather live in a smaller house with a payment I can handle than a nicer one that scares me.

say: I'd say five years is a gap but **not a big one**, and employers should show plans.
At work I'd ask directly what our desk looks like in **2031**.
I'd tell friends to **save** and keep options open.
think: I'd still expect my desk to go, but I'd have **time to get ahead**.
The worry is that the **whole sector** would be moving at once.
do: I'd try the software in year one to see where I'm still **useful**.
I'd ask the company to retrain me for **trade counter** or customer-facing work.
I'd buy a house only with a **bigger deposit** and safe-looking jobs.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to cope, with some control.
S3.quote: I'd rather live in a smaller house with a payment I can handle than a nicer one that scares me.
fieldNote: The extra time makes him **proactive** but still doubtful about his own desk.
He relies on **personal contacts** at mills and builders for his next job.
The house plan stays alive but is **made smaller and safer**.

steps.text: Try the ordering software to find where my judgment still matters
Ask to retrain for the trade counter or customer sales
Buy a smaller house with a bigger deposit
Keep saving a quarter of my pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds long enough to sort things out calmly. I'd say at work that we should plan in stages and not make big announcements. I'd tell friends it's a good moment to build skills and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but not scared. I'd be thirty-seven, probably in a more senior role, and I'd have time to move into something less exposed. What I'd fear is getting comfortable and then finding that ten years passed quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my role, learn the software gradually and keep my relationships alive. I'd buy the house, start a family with Leila, and put aside a bigger sum for a possible change of career. I might also take an evening course in business management, which would help if I moved into running a yard or a branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly relaxed with a small knot of worry. Ten years feels like a long road, but I know how fast roads go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years might pass quickly. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a check every year, just an evening with Leila and a spreadsheet. We'd look at savings, my skills, and what changed at work. If nothing changed in a year, we'd ask why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a family fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably have children around thirty-one. I'd want to have the house sorted and over a year of savings in the bank first, so nobody's under pressure. A decade's warning makes me more willing to go ahead, not less.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough to **sort things out calmly**.
At work I'd suggest planning in **stages**.
I'd tell friends to build **skills and savings** now.
think: I'd be **uneasy but not scared**, and at 37 I'd have time to move.
I'd fear getting **comfortable** and finding ten years passed quickly.
do: I'd stay in my role and learn the software **gradually**.
I'd buy the house and start a **family** with Leila around thirty-one.
I'd take an evening **business management** course for a future yard or branch role.
feel: I feel **fairly relaxed** with a small knot of worry.
S4.quote: A decade's warning makes me more willing to go ahead, not less.
fieldNote: The decade **relaxes** his resistance and lets him plan a family.
He fears **comfort** more than the technology.
An annual check with Leila is his **safeguard** against drift.

steps.text: Learn the ordering software gradually, one task at a time
Have children around thirty-one once the house is sorted
Take an evening business management course
Buy the house with a large deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question, because I'm in the group the card describes: desk, phone, spreadsheets. What would help is something practical, like a retraining scheme that actually leads to a job, and a firm that gives a year's notice instead of a week. I'm not asking for a handout, just for a fair shot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd change. Everyone assumes I'm stubborn, and I am, but I also know that sticking to what's familiar has been a choice and not a rule. If someone showed me a tool that saved me an evening a week, I'd probably try it.

headlineQuote: I also know that sticking to what's familiar has been a choice and not a rule.
portrait: Jamal is a 27-year-old senior buyer at a **builders' supply** distributor, with a master's degree and a steady head.
He is centrist and resistant to new technology: he keeps a **paper stock sheet** and has never used AI tools.
His main worry is the **building cycle**, since a downturn hits the buyers' desk first, whatever AI does.
His girlfriend Leila is a **dental hygienist** and his parents run a corner shop, which is his safety net.
He expects the desk to go in the fast scenarios, so he looks for **hands-on roles** in the yard.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, since desk and phone work is the group the card describes.
whatWouldHelp: A retraining scheme that **leads to a job**, not a handout.
A year of **notice** from employers instead of a week.
